learningObjectives.title: Germany and the growth of democracy, 1890-1929 (Kaiser, the First World War and Weimar democracy)
Germany and the Depression, 1929-1933 (impact of the Depression, failure of Weimar and Hitler's rise to power)
The Nazi dictatorship: the police state, terror and propaganda
The experiences of Germans under the Nazis: economy, women and youth

questions.q: Who was the ruler (Kaiser) of the German Empire from 1888 until 1918?
options: Wilhelm II
Otto von Bismarck
Friedrich Ebert
Paul von Hindenburg
questions.explain: Kaiser Wilhelm II ruled the German Empire from 1888 until he abdicated in November 1918.

questions.q: What was the name of the elected national parliament in Germany before 1918?
options: The Reichstag
The Bundestag
The Duma
The Landtag
questions.explain: The Reichstag was the elected parliament, though real power under the Kaiser lay with the monarch and Chancellor.

questions.q: Why did the growing support for the SPD worry the Kaiser before 1914?
options: It wanted the Reichstag to have more power at the Kaiser's expense
It demanded a much larger navy than Britain's
It wished to restore the monarchy's absolute power
It supported an immediate war against France
questions.explain: The SPD backed democratic reform, threatening the Kaiser's autocratic control of government.

questions.q: In which month and year did Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicate?
options: November 1918
November 1919
August 1914
January 1933
questions.explain: Facing revolution and defeat in the First World War, the Kaiser abdicated in November 1918, leading to the Weimar Republic.

questions.q: What did Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allow the President to do?
options: Rule by emergency decree without the Reichstag's consent
Dissolve all political parties permanently
Appoint the Kaiser as head of state
Abolish the right to vote for women
questions.explain: Article 48 let the President govern by decree in an emergency, a weakness later exploited to undermine democracy.

questions.q: Which 1919 treaty forced Germany to accept blame for the war and pay reparations?
options: The Treaty of Versailles
The Treaty of Locarno
The Dawes Plan
The Treaty of Rapallo
questions.explain: The Treaty of Versailles imposed the War Guilt clause, reparations and territorial losses on Germany.

questions.q: What was the main cause of the hyperinflation crisis of 1923?
options: French occupation of the Ruhr and the government printing money
A sudden fall in the world price of gold
The signing of the Locarno treaties
An invasion of Germany by the Soviet Union
questions.explain: When France occupied the Ruhr, Germany printed money to pay striking workers, destroying the value of the mark.

questions.q: Who became Chancellor in 1923 and introduced a new currency to end hyperinflation?
options: Gustav Stresemann
Friedrich Ebert
Adolf Hitler
Heinrich Bruning
questions.explain: Stresemann introduced the Rentenmark in 1923, helping to stabilise the German economy.

questions.q: What was the main effect of the Dawes Plan of 1924?
options: It provided US loans and rescheduled reparations, aiding recovery
It cancelled all of Germany's reparations completely
It removed Germany from the League of Nations
It doubled the size of the German army
questions.explain: The Dawes Plan brought American loans and easier reparation terms, helping the Weimar economy recover after 1924.

questions.q: Which event in October 1929 triggered a worldwide economic depression that hit Germany hard?
options: The Wall Street Crash
The Munich Putsch
The Reichstag Fire
The Night of the Long Knives
questions.explain: The Wall Street Crash led to the recall of US loans and mass unemployment in Germany.

questions.q: Why did the Depression increase support for the Nazi Party after 1929?
options: Rising unemployment made people turn to parties promising strong solutions
The Nazis promised to keep paying reparations in full
German living standards were rising rapidly at the time
The Nazis were the only party allowed to campaign
questions.explain: Mass unemployment and fear of communism led many desperate Germans to back the Nazis' promises of work and order.

questions.q: An unemployed factory worker in 1932 fears both poverty and communism. Which Nazi promise would most likely appeal to him?
options: Work and a strong, revived Germany
The return of the Kaiser to power
Continued reparations payments to the Allies
Immediate disarmament of the German army
questions.explain: Nazi propaganda targeted such fears by pledging jobs, national pride and protection from communism.

questions.q: On what date was Adolf Hitler appointed Chancellor of Germany?
options: 30 January 1933
9 November 1923
28 June 1919
2 August 1934
questions.explain: President Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933, believing he could be controlled.

questions.q: How did Hitler use the Reichstag Fire of February 1933?
options: To pass an emergency decree and arrest communist opponents
To declare himself Kaiser of Germany
To cancel the Treaty of Versailles
To restore full powers to the Reichstag
questions.explain: The fire was blamed on communists, letting Hitler suspend civil rights and crush opposition before the election.

questions.q: The Nazis claimed the Enabling Act of March 1933 was legal because the Reichstag passed it. What did it actually allow Hitler to do?
options: Make laws for four years without the Reichstag or President
Ban the German army permanently
Hold free multi-party elections every two years
Share power equally with the SPD
questions.explain: The Enabling Act let Hitler rule by decree, effectively ending democracy and establishing his dictatorship.

questions.q: What was the name of the Nazi secret state police?
options: The Gestapo
The SA
The Reichstag
The Luftwaffe
questions.explain: The Gestapo was the secret police used to spy on, arrest and terrorise opponents of the Nazi regime.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of the Night of the Long Knives in June 1934?
options: To remove Rohm and the SA leadership and win the army's loyalty
To invade Poland and start the Second World War
To hold Germany's first free elections
To arrest all Jewish citizens of Germany
questions.explain: Hitler purged Rohm and SA leaders he saw as rivals, securing the support of the regular army.

questions.q: The Nazis staged the 1936 Berlin Olympics with grand stadiums and organisation. What was their main aim in doing so?
options: To present a positive, powerful image of Nazi Germany to the world
To secretly recruit foreign soldiers into the army
To raise money to pay reparations
To encourage other countries to adopt democracy
questions.explain: Goebbels used the Olympics as propaganda to showcase Nazi strength, order and efficiency internationally.

questions.q: What did the Nazi slogan 'Kinder, Kuche, Kirche' express about the role of women?
options: That women belonged at home caring for children, cooking and church
That women should lead the army and government
That women should work in heavy industry
That women should not marry or have children
questions.explain: Nazi ideology promoted 'children, kitchen, church', encouraging women to be homemakers and mothers.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy in 1937 attends meetings with camping, fitness and Nazi ideology to prepare him for future military service. Which organisation is this?
options: The Hitler Youth
The League of German Maidens
The Gestapo
The German Labour Front
questions.explain: The Hitler Youth trained boys physically and ideologically to become loyal Nazis and future soldiers.
